anatomy.lede: The greater blue-ringed octopus is about the size of a golf ball, and its whole skin is a warning sign.

hotspots.label: Blue ring
hotspots.text: The rings are 7 to 8 mm across, larger than in other blue-ringed octopuses, which helps tell this species apart. Each is bordered by a black line that sharpens the contrast.

hotspots.label: Dark blotch
hotspots.text: Dark chromatophores sit beneath and around each ring to boost contrast. Unusually for a cephalopod, there are none on top of the ring.

hotspots.label: Eye
hotspots.text: Blue lines run through the eyes, a characteristic marking of this species.

hotspots.label: Mantle
hotspots.text: The background colour changes with its surroundings and mood, from yellow ochre to light brown, or whitish when the octopus is inactive.

hotspots.label: Arms
hotspots.text: The eight arms are relatively short. It hunts by pouncing on prey, seizing it with its arms and pulling it to its beak.

body.lede: The blue-ringed octopus carries enough poison to kill a person, and it has evolved ways to show it off and to survive it.

systems.title: Rings on a switch
systems.text: Each ring contains inert multilayer reflectors tucked into a pouch of skin. Relaxing muscles above the reflectors and contracting muscles around the ring opens the pouch and flashes the blue.

systems.title: Poison throughout the body
systems.text: TTX is concentrated in the posterior salivary gland but also lies just under the skin of the mantle and arms and in channels through the dermis. Its presence in blood-rich organs such as the gills and hearts suggests it is carried in the blood.

systems.title: Immune to its own poison
systems.text: TTX works by blocking sodium channels in nerves. This octopus has three amino-acid changes in its sodium channel that reduce TTX binding, matching changes that evolved separately in TTX-bearing fish and salamanders.

systems.title: Two kinds of venom
systems.text: Its saliva carries the products of two kinds of venom glands: one used to subdue crustacean prey, and tetrodotoxin, thought to serve mainly for defence.

mind.lede: Most of the time this octopus is hidden and camouflaged. Its most dramatic behaviour, the ring flash, is reserved for emergencies.

studies.title: How the rings flash
studies.text: Bathing the skin in chemicals that act on colour cells did not change the rings, showing the blue comes from fixed reflectors. The fast flashes are driven by muscles under direct nerve control, a mechanism not reported before in cephalopods.

studies.title: Mating blind
studies.text: Whether one octopus touches another does not depend on sex, size or who lives there. Male–female matings last about 160 minutes, but male–male encounters about 30 seconds, suggesting a male cannot tell the sex of his partner until he inserts his mating arm.

studies.title: A tidy doorway
studies.text: Like other octopuses it lives in a den, and the entrance is easy to spot because it is littered with empty shells and crab legs from past meals.

survival.lede: The blue-ringed octopus hides first, warns second and bites only as a last resort.

tactics.title: Camouflage
tactics.text: It spends much of its time hidden, showing effective camouflage patterns.

tactics.title: Warning flash
tactics.text: When disturbed it flashes its rings, an exceptionally fast and conspicuous warning display.

tactics.title: A deadly bite
tactics.text: Strongly harassed, it bites and can deliver a neurotoxin able to kill a person. The bite is painless, and no antidote is known.

life.lede: A blue-ringed octopus lives fast: it hatches the size of a pea, is mating by the following autumn and dies after breeding.

stages.name: Egg
stages.text: The female lays about 50 to 100 eggs and carries them under her arms until they hatch, without feeding.

stages.name: Paralarva
stages.text: Hatchlings are about the size of a pea and drift briefly in the plankton before settling on the seabed.

stages.name: Juvenile
stages.text: Young octopuses grow quickly on the reef, rubble and sand of shallow coasts, feeding on small crabs, shrimps and molluscs.

stages.name: Adult
stages.text: They mature quickly and begin mating the following autumn. Males die after mating, and females die soon after their eggs hatch.
